title: Quantum fluctuation-driven transport crossover between two liquid states in distinguishable helium-4
authors: Mika Tanabe, Momoko Tsujimoto, Kenichi Kinugawa
abstract: We show the emergence of a quantum fluctuation-driven transport crossover between two liquid states in distinguishable helium-4 obeying Boltzmann statistics, in the absence of atomic exchange. Using path integral centroid molecular dynamics simulations over 0.1-3.3 K and 1-60 bar, we investigate the transport properties of two distinct liquid states: the low quantum-dispersion liquid (LQDL) and the high quantum-dispersion liquid (HQDL). While LQDL exhibits conventional liquid behavior consistent with the Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, HQDL emerges at lower temperatures and displays anomalous gas-like transport characterized by superdiffusion and ultralow viscosity, accompanied by a breakdown of the SE relation. This counterintuitive emergence of gas-like dynamics upon cooling reflects the dominant role of nuclear quantum fluctuations, in contrast to thermal fluctuations at higher temperatures. Across the LQDL-HQDL boundary, we identify a transport crossover marked by a qualitative change in the velocity autocorrelation function (VAF), a transition in the Prandtl number, and the emergence of transport minima in shear and kinematic viscosities, thermal conductivity, and thermal diffusivity. These minima reflect a crossover from liquid-like to gas-like transport upon cooling in the low-temperature subcritical region, in addition to the universal transport minima observed in the supercritical regime. The transition from oscillatory to monotonic VAF defines a second Frenkel line, distinct from the conventional Frenkel line observed in the supercritical region. LQDL is a heat-transport-dominated dissipative fluid, whereas HQDL is a momentum-dominated inertial fluid. These results demonstrate that nuclear quantum fluctuations alone induce gas-like liquid behavior and provide a unified picture of transport phenomena in distinguishable helium-4 without superfluidity.
summary: This work uses advanced molecular dynamics simulations to study the transport behavior of distinguishable helium-4 across two distinct liquid states: LQDL and HQDL. The key finding is that cooling induces a crossover into an anomalous, gas-like state (HQDL) due to quantum fluctuations alone. This provides a unified picture of quantum fluid dynamics without relying on superfluidity.
main_problem: The study investigates a quantum fluctuation-driven transport crossover between two distinct liquid states (LQDL and HQDL) in distinguishable helium-4, specifically isolating effects from nuclear quantum fluctuations.
main_result: The system exhibits a transition across the LQDL-HQDL boundary marked by anomalous gas-like dynamics (superdiffusion, ultralow viscosity) emerging upon cooling, driven solely by NQEs without invoking superfluidity.
method: Path Integral Centroid Molecular Dynamics (CMD) simulations were employed to calculate various transport properties using the Green-Kubo formalism.
model_or_system: The system is distinguishable Helium-4 atoms obeying Boltzmann statistics. The simulation maps the quantum problem onto classical polymers via centroid coordinates, allowing investigation of two liquid states: Low Quantum-Dispersion Liquid (LQDL) and High Quantum-Dispersion Liquid (HQDL).
key_observables: Self-diffusion coefficient (D), shear viscosity ($\eta_s$), thermal conductivity ($\lambda$), Velocity Autocorrelation Function (VAF), and the Prandtl number.
important_parameters: Temperature range ($0.1–3.3 	ext{ K}$) and pressure range ($1–60 	ext{ bar}$); quantum wavelength ($\lambda_{	ext{quantum}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed phenomena are driven solely by nuclear quantum fluctuations (NQEs) in a distinguishable particle framework, avoiding Bose statistics considerations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate snapshots showing spatial delocalization differences between LQDL and HQDL states based on $\lambda_{	ext{quantum}}$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes transport properties across varying P-T conditions to map the crossover boundary. Key diagnostics include monitoring VAF changes, Prandtl number transitions, and identifying minima in various transport coefficients.
why_interesting: It provides a detailed quantum mechanical description of liquid dynamics far from equilibrium, offering insights into how fundamental quantum statistics (like NQEs) dictate macroscopic transport properties even when superfluidity is absent.
